entries.lesson_core_move: Verify causality of an LTI system by checking that its impulse response satisfies h(t)=0 for all t<0 in the pole-based stability setting.

sections.section_title: Checking h(t)=0 for t<0 from an Impulse Response Formula

prompt_blocks.text: Given $h(t)=2u(t)-3u(t-1)+u(-t-2)$, is the system causal or noncausal?

choice_blocks.text: Noncausal, because $u(-t-2)$ is nonzero for $t<-2$.
Causal, because every term contains a unit step and therefore vanishes for $t<0$.
Causal, because $u(-t-2)=0$ for every negative $t$.
Noncausal, because $u(t-1)$ creates negative-time support.
Causal, because the coefficients are finite and the response is bounded.

questions.correct_answer: Noncausal, because $u(-t-2)$ is nonzero for $t<-2$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The term $u(-t-2)$ is active when $-t-2\ge 0$, so it is nonzero for $t\le -2$. That gives a negative-time interval where $h(t)\neq 0$, which violates the causality test $h(t)=0$ for all $t<0$.

prompt_blocks.text: Given $h(t)=4e^{-t}u(t)+u(-t+1)-2u(t-3)$, is the system causal or noncausal?

choice_blocks.text: Noncausal, because $u(-t+1)$ is nonzero for some $t<0$.
Causal, because the right-shifted term $u(t-3)$ makes the response one-sided.
Noncausal, because $4e^{-t}u(t)$ grows for $t<0$.
Causal, because $u(-t+1)$ only matters at $t=0$.
Causal, because the response decays for positive time.

questions.correct_answer: Noncausal, because $u(-t+1)$ is nonzero for some $t<0$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The term $u(-t+1)$ is active when $-t+1\ge 0$, so it is nonzero for $t\le 1$. That includes negative-time values such as $t=-1$, where the impulse response is already nonzero, so the system is noncausal.

sections.section_title: Checking Causality from an Impulse Response Graph

image_slots.image_description: Graph of $h(t)$ versus t with clear $t$- and $h(t)$-axes, a short nonzero pulse on a negative-time interval around $t=-1.2$ to $t=-0.8$, and a right-sided exponential tail for $t\ge 0$; no other negative-time support.
Graph of $h(t)$ versus t with clear $t$- and $h(t)$-axes, a single impulse-like spike at $t=0$, a right-sided exponential tail for $t>0$, and zero response for all $t<0$.

prompt_blocks.text: Use the graph of $h(t)$ below to decide whether the system is causal or noncausal.

choice_blocks.text: Causal, because the graph has no nonzero support for $t<0$.
Noncausal, because the graph has a nonzero pulse on a negative-time interval.
Causal, because the left-side pulse is really on $t>0$ if the time axis is read backward.
Noncausal, because the right-sided exponential tail alone makes the system noncausal.
Causal, because isolated negative-time spikes do not count in the support test.

questions.correct_answer: Noncausal, because the graph has a nonzero pulse on a negative-time interval.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A continuous-time LTI system is causal only when $h(t)=0$ for every $t<0$. This graph has a nonzero pulse on a negative-time interval, so the impulse response is not zero for all $t<0$ and the system is noncausal.

prompt_blocks.text: Use the graph of $h(t)$ below to decide whether the system is causal or noncausal.

choice_blocks.text: Causal, because there is no nonzero support for $t<0$, and the spike at $t=0$ is allowed.
Noncausal, because any nonzero value at $t=0$ makes the system noncausal.
Noncausal, because the right-sided exponential tail means the system depends on future inputs.
Noncausal, because the graph is bilaterally supported.
Causal, because the spike at $t=0$ should be treated as negative-time support.

questions.correct_answer: Causal, because there is no nonzero support for $t<0$, and the spike at $t=0$ is allowed.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Causality depends only on whether $h(t)$ is zero for all $t<0$. This graph has no negative-time support, so the system is causal. A spike at $t=0$ does not violate the causality test.

sections.section_title: Identifying Noncausal Negative-Time Support

prompt_blocks.text: Identify the negative-time support of $h(t)=e^{-t}u(t-2)+\frac{1}{2}\big(u(-t+1)-u(-t-4)\big)$ and classify causality.

choice_blocks.text: Causal; support on $[2,\infty)$.
Noncausal; support on $(-4,0)$.
Noncausal; support on $(-\infty,0)$.
Noncausal; support on $(-\infty,2]$.
Causal; support on $(-4,0)$.

questions.correct_answer: Noncausal; support on $(-4,0)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The windowed difference $u(-t+1)-u(-t-4)$ is nonzero for $-4<t\le 1$, so it produces negative-time support on $(-4,0)$. Since $h(t)$ is nonzero for some $t<0$, the system is noncausal. The $e^{-t}u(t-2)$ term is right-sided and does not change that conclusion.

prompt_blocks.text: Identify the negative-time support of $h(t)=3u(t)-u(t-2)+\frac{3}{4}u(-t-4)$ and classify causality.

choice_blocks.text: Causal; support on $[0,\infty)$.
Noncausal; support on $(-\infty,-4]$.
Noncausal; support on $[-4,\infty)$.
Noncausal; support on $(-\infty,2]$.
Causal; support on $(-\infty,-4]$.

questions.correct_answer: Noncausal; support on $(-\infty,-4]$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The term $u(-t-4)$ is active when $t\le -4$, so the impulse response is nonzero on negative time. That alone makes the system noncausal. The right-sided terms $3u(t)$ and $-u(t-2)$ do not remove the left-sided support.

sections.section_title: Verifying Causality Before Using Pole Locations

prompt_blocks.text: Given $H(s)=\frac{s+2}{s(s+1)(s+4)}$, which step comes first before using pole locations to conclude BIBO stability?

choice_blocks.text: Verify causality from $h(t)$ first; if a noncausal term appears, stop before the pole test.
Check only the pole locations because rational transfer functions are always causal.
Conclude BIBO stable immediately because all poles are in the left half-plane.
Test BIBO stability first and infer causality from the result afterward.
Declare the system noncausal because the transfer function has a zero at $s=-2$.

questions.correct_answer: Verify causality from $h(t)$ first; if a noncausal term appears, stop before the pole test.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: This lesson requires the time-domain causality check before any pole-location conclusion. Pole locations are only used after $h(t)$ has been verified to satisfy $h(t)=0$ for all $t<0$.

prompt_blocks.text: Suppose the inverse transform gives $h(t)=e^{-2t}u(t)-3u(-t-1)$. What should you conclude before any pole-location stability check?

choice_blocks.text: Causal, because the $e^{-2t}u(t)$ term is right-sided and dominates.
Noncausal, because the $u(-t-1)$ term is nonzero for some $t<0$, so the pole test should not be used yet.
Stable, because the negative exponent guarantees BIBO stability.
Causal, because any unit-step term makes the response right-sided.
Noncausal only if the poles are in the right half-plane.

questions.correct_answer: Noncausal, because the $u(-t-1)$ term is nonzero for some $t<0$, so the pole test should not be used yet.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Any nonzero negative-time term breaks causality. Since $u(-t-1)$ is active for $t\le -1$, the impulse response is noncausal, and this lesson says to stop before using pole locations.

entries.lesson_core_move: Classify a causal LTI system as BIBO stable or unstable by checking whether every transfer-function pole lies strictly in the left half of the s-plane.

sections.section_title: Classifying a Causal LTI System from Listed Pole Locations

prompt_blocks.text: A causal LTI system has transfer-function poles $p=\{-1,-2,-4\}$. Which statement correctly applies the BIBO pole test?

choice_blocks.text: BIBO stable, because every pole satisfies $\Re\{p_i\}<0$.
BIBO unstable, because at least one pole has negative real part.
BIBO unstable, because stability depends on pole magnitude $|p_i|$ rather than real part sign.
BIBO stable, because zeros, not poles, determine the stability test.
BIBO unstable, because the pole $p=-4$ is farthest from the origin.

questions.correct_answer: BIBO stable, because all listed poles satisfy $\Re\{p_i\}<0$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: For a causal LTI system, BIBO stability requires every transfer-function pole to lie strictly in the left half-plane. The poles $-1$, $-2$, and $-4$ all have negative real parts, so the system is BIBO stable.

prompt_blocks.text: A causal LTI system has transfer-function poles $p=\{-3,-1+j2,-1-j2,0\}$. Which statement correctly applies the BIBO pole test?

choice_blocks.text: BIBO stable, because no pole has positive real part.
BIBO unstable, because the pole at $0$ does not satisfy $\Re\{p_i\}<0$.
BIBO stable, because the complex poles have negative real parts and their imaginary parts do not matter.
BIBO unstable, because the complex poles have nonzero imaginary parts.
BIBO stable, because the pole magnitudes are finite.

questions.correct_answer: BIBO unstable, because one pole is at $0$, so not every pole has $\Re\{p_i\}<0$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The strict causal BIBO stability test is that every pole must have negative real part. The poles $-3$ and $-1\pm j2$ satisfy the test, but the pole at $0$ has real part $0$, not a negative real part. Therefore the system is BIBO unstable.

sections.section_title: Classifying Stability from a Factored Transfer Function

prompt_blocks.text: Classify the BIBO stability of $H(s)=\dfrac{3(s+1)}{(s+1)(s+4)(s+5)}$ for a causal LTI system.

choice_blocks.text: BIBO stable, because the denominator poles are $-1$, $-4$, and $-5$.
BIBO unstable, because the numerator zero at $s=-1$ appears in the denominator.
BIBO unstable, because the pole from $(s+1)$ is $s=1$.
Not BIBO stable, because strict stability requires every pole to satisfy $\Re(p)>0$.
BIBO stable, because the numerator has a zero at $s=-1$.

questions.correct_answer: BIBO stable, because the denominator poles are $-1$, $-4$, and $-5$, and each satisfies $\Re(p)<0$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: For BIBO stability of a causal LTI system, inspect the denominator factors. The factors $(s+1)$, $(s+4)$, and $(s+5)$ give poles $-1$, $-4$, and $-5$.
All three poles are strictly in the left half-plane, so the system is BIBO stable.

prompt_blocks.text: Classify the BIBO stability of $H(s)=\dfrac{5(s+2)}{(s+3)(s-1)(s+7)}$ for a causal LTI system.

choice_blocks.text: BIBO stable, because the numerator zero is at $s=-2$.
BIBO unstable, because one denominator pole is $s=1$.
BIBO stable, because the denominator poles have finite magnitudes $1$, $3$, and $7$.
BIBO stable, because two denominator poles are negative.
Not enough information, because BIBO stability cannot be classified from denominator factors.

questions.correct_answer: BIBO unstable, because the denominator factor $(s-1)$ gives the pole $s=1$, which has $\Re(p)>0$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use the denominator factors to find the poles. The factors $(s+3)$, $(s-1)$, and $(s+7)$ give poles $-3$, $1$, and $-7$.
Because the pole $s=1$ is in the right half-plane, not every pole satisfies $\Re(p)<0$. The causal system is therefore BIBO unstable.

sections.section_title: Classifying Stability from a Pole-Zero Plot

image_slots.image_description: Create an s-plane pole-zero plot with horizontal real axis labeled Re(s) and vertical imaginary axis labeled Im(s). Show pole markers (x) at s=-3, s=-0.5+1.5j, and s=-0.5-1.5j. Show zero markers (o) at s=1.5 and s=-2j. Use a coordinate grid and lightly shade or label the left half-plane and right half-plane; keep a small note that BIBO stability depends only on pole real parts.

Create an s-plane pole-zero plot with horizontal real axis labeled Re(s) and vertical imaginary axis labeled Im(s). Show pole markers (x) at s=-2, s=-1-j1, and s=+j1 on the imaginary axis. Show zero markers (o) at s=-3 and s=2. Use a coordinate grid and lightly shade or label the left half-plane and right half-plane; make the imaginary-axis pole visually clear because the strict left-half-plane test is the key.

prompt_blocks.text: Use the pole-zero plot for a causal LTI system. Which option correctly classifies BIBO stability?

choice_blocks.text: BIBO stable; all plotted poles have $\Re(p)<0$.
BIBO unstable; the zero at $s=1.5$ is in the right half-plane.
BIBO unstable; the pole closest to the imaginary axis controls by distance only.
BIBO stable; zeros cancel the pole-location test.
BIBO unstable; stability requires every zero to be in the left half-plane.

questions.correct_answer: BIBO stable because every pole is strictly in the left half-plane.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The poles are at $-3$ and $-0.5\pm j1.5$, so every pole has negative real part. The right-half-plane zero does not affect the causal BIBO pole test, so the system is BIBO stable.

prompt_blocks.text: Use the pole-zero plot for a causal LTI system. Which option correctly classifies BIBO stability?

choice_blocks.text: BIBO stable; no pole is strictly in the right half-plane.
BIBO unstable; the pole on the imaginary axis is not strictly in the left half-plane.
BIBO stable; the left-half-plane zero makes the system stable.
BIBO unstable; the right-half-plane zero determines the classification.
BIBO stable; poles on the imaginary axis satisfy $\Re(p)<0$.

questions.correct_answer: BIBO unstable because one pole lies on the imaginary axis.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The pole at $j1$ has real part $0$, not a strictly negative real part. Since causal BIBO stability requires every pole to satisfy $\Re(p)<0$, the system is BIBO unstable even though no pole is to the right of the imaginary axis.

sections.section_title: Detecting Instability from One Pole Outside the Strict Left Half-Plane

prompt_blocks.text: Classify the BIBO stability of $H(s)=\dfrac{1}{(s+1)(s+4)(s-2)}$.

choice_blocks.text: Stable because two of the three poles are in the left half-plane.
Unstable because the pole at $s=2$ is in the right half-plane.
Stable because the stability test uses $\Re(p)\le 0$ for every pole.
Stable because the numerator has no finite zeros.
Unstable only if the right-half-plane pole is repeated.

questions.correct_answer: Unstable because the denominator has a pole at $s=2$, and $\Re(2)>0$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The denominator factors give poles $-1$, $-4$, and $2$. BIBO stability for this causal LTI system requires every pole to satisfy $\Re(p)<0$. Since $2$ is in the right half-plane, one pole violates the strict condition, so the system is unstable.

prompt_blocks.text: Classify the BIBO stability of $H(s)=\dfrac{3}{s(s+2)(s+6)}$.

choice_blocks.text: Stable because the pole at $s=0$ satisfies $\Re(p)\le 0$.
Unstable because the pole at $s=0$ is not strictly in the left half-plane.
Stable because the two negative poles dominate the pole at the origin.
Stable because only zeros, not poles, determine BIBO stability.
Unstable only if there are more nonnegative poles than negative poles.

questions.correct_answer: Unstable because the pole at $s=0$ has $\Re(0)=0$, which is outside the strict left half-plane.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The denominator gives poles $0$, $-2$, and $-6$. The strict criterion is $\Re(p)<0$ for every pole. The pole at $0$ lies on the imaginary axis rather than in the strict left half-plane, so the system is not BIBO stable.

entries.lesson_core_move: Recognize left-half-plane poles by using their negative real parts to identify decaying response modes that support BIBO stability in causal LTI systems.

sections.section_title: Identifying Poles with Negative Real Parts

prompt_blocks.text: Given the pole set $\{-3, 0, 2, -0.5+j1\}$ for a causal LTI system, which classification is correct?

choice_blocks.text: BIBO stable, because three of the poles have negative real parts.
Not BIBO stable, because the pole at $0$ is on the boundary and the pole at $2$ is in the right half-plane.
BIBO stable, because the complex pole $-0.5+j1$ has a nonzero imaginary part.
Not BIBO stable, because stability depends on the imaginary part instead of the real part.
BIBO stable, because any negative pole is enough to make a causal LTI system stable.

questions.correct_answer: Not BIBO stable.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Check the real parts pole by pole: $-3$, $0$, $2$, and $-0.5$. The strict BIBO test requires every pole to satisfy $\Re\{p\}<0$, and the poles at $0$ and $2$ fail that test.

prompt_blocks.text: Given the pole set $\{-4, -4, -0.5+j3, -0.5-j3\}$ for a causal LTI system, which classification is correct?

choice_blocks.text: Not BIBO stable, because the repeated pole at $-4$ counts twice.
BIBO stable, because every pole has negative real part.
Not BIBO stable, because complex poles are never allowed in the left half-plane.
Not BIBO stable, because the imaginary parts are nonzero.
BIBO stable, because repeated poles are stable even if one pole were on the boundary.

questions.correct_answer: BIBO stable.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The repeated pole at $-4$ still satisfies the same sign test as a single pole, and the complex conjugate pair has real part $-0.5$. Since every pole has $\Re\{p\}<0$, the causal LTI system is BIBO stable.

sections.section_title: Locating Left-Half-Plane Poles on the s-Plane

image_slots.image_description: A pole-zero-style $s$-plane map with real axis labeled Re(s) and imaginary axis labeled Im(s). Show poles at $s=-2$, $s=-0.5$, $s=0.2$, and $s=-1+2j$, plus zero markers at $s=\pm j2$. Make the imaginary-axis boundary clear and the coordinates legible.

A pole-zero-style $s$-plane map with real axis labeled Re(s) and imaginary axis labeled Im(s). Show poles at $s=-2$, $s=-0.5$, $s=0$, and $s=-1+2j$, plus zero markers at $s=\pm j2$. Make the imaginary-axis boundary clear and the coordinates legible.

prompt_blocks.text: Use the pole map to identify the left-half-plane poles and choose the correct stability conclusion for the causal system.
Focus on poles only. The zeros on the imaginary axis are distractors here.

choice_blocks.text: LHP poles are $\{-2,\,-0.5,\,0.2,\,-1+2j\}$, so the system is BIBO stable.
LHP poles are $\{-2,\,-0.5,\,-1+2j\}$, so the system is not BIBO stable because of the pole at $0.2$.
LHP poles are $\{-2,\,-0.5,\,-1+2j\}$, so the system is BIBO stable because the zeros lie on the imaginary axis.
LHP poles are $\{-2,\,0.2,\,-1+2j\}$, so the system is not BIBO stable because the pole at $-0.5$ is a zero.
LHP poles are $\{-2,\,-0.5,\,-1+2j\}$, so the system is stable because any complex pole counts as left-half-plane.

questions.correct_answer: B

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Read the pole coordinates and apply the strict rule $\Re\{s\}<0$.
The left-half-plane poles are $\{-2,\,-0.5,\,-1+2j\}$. The pole at $0.2$ has positive real part, so the all-poles test fails and the causal LTI system is not BIBO stable.

prompt_blocks.text: Use the pole map to identify the left-half-plane poles and choose the correct stability conclusion for the causal system.
Again, ignore the zeros and use only pole locations for the stability decision.

choice_blocks.text: LHP poles are $\{-2,\,-0.5,\,-1+2j,\,0\}$, so the system is BIBO stable.
LHP poles are $\{-2,\,-0.5,\,-1+2j\}$, so the system is BIBO stable because a pole at $0$ is still allowed.
LHP poles are $\{-2,\,-0.5,\,0\}$, so the system is not BIBO stable because the complex pole is ignored.
LHP poles are $\{-2,\,-0.5,\,-1+2j\}$, so the system is not BIBO stable because the pole at $0$ lies on the imaginary axis and fails $\Re\{s\}<0$.
LHP poles are $\{-2,\,-0.5,\,-1+2j\}$, so the system is not BIBO stable because zeros at $\pm j2$ are unstable.

questions.correct_answer: D

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Apply the same strict left-half-plane rule to the plotted poles.
The left-half-plane poles are $\{-2,\,-0.5,\,-1+2j\}$. The pole at $0$ sits on the imaginary axis, so it fails the strict inequality $\Re\{s\}<0$ and the causal LTI system is not BIBO stable.

sections.section_title: Interpreting Negative Real Parts as Decaying Modes

prompt_blocks.text: For poles $s=-1$ and $s=-2+3j$, which statement about the associated modes is correct?

choice_blocks.text: Both modes decay, and the $s=-2+3j$ mode decays faster because its real part is more negative.
The $s=-2+3j$ mode does not decay because the nonzero imaginary part makes it oscillatory.
The $s=-1$ mode decays faster because $|-1|<|-2|$.
The $s=-2+3j$ mode grows because the imaginary part is larger than the real part.
Both modes are non-decaying because every complex pole is unstable.

questions.correct_answer: Both modes decay, and the $s=-2+3j$ mode decays faster because its real part is more negative.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Write each pole as $s=\sigma+j\omega$ and look at the factor $e^{\sigma t}$. Here $\sigma=-1$ and $\sigma=-2$, so both modes decay. The more negative real part decays faster, and the imaginary part only adds oscillation.

prompt_blocks.text: For poles $s=-0.2+4j$ and $s=0.1$, which statement about the associated modes is correct?

choice_blocks.text: Both modes decay because one pole is complex and the other is real.
Only the $s=-0.2+4j$ mode decays; the $s=0.1$ mode grows because its real part is positive.
Both modes decay, and the $s=0.1$ mode decays faster because a smaller positive number is closer to zero.
The $s=-0.2+4j$ mode is non-decaying because the imaginary part is large.
The $s=0.1$ mode decays because real poles always decay if they are close to zero.

questions.correct_answer: Only the $s=-0.2+4j$ mode decays; the $s=0.1$ mode grows because its real part is positive.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A mode decays only when the real part $\sigma$ is negative. For $-0.2+4j$, $\sigma=-0.2$, so the mode decays with oscillation. For $0.1$, $\sigma=0.1>0$, so the mode grows and is not bounded.

sections.section_title: Connecting All Left-Half-Plane Poles to BIBO Stability

prompt_blocks.text: Determine BIBO stability of $H(s)=\frac{6}{(s+1)^2(s+0.2)(s+3)}$ for a causal LTI system.

choice_blocks.text: BIBO stable because every pole has negative real part, even though one pole is repeated.
Unstable because repeated poles are never stable.
Unstable because the pole at $-0.2$ is too close to the imaginary axis.
BIBO stable because the numerator is constant, so there are no zeros to worry about.
Unstable because the poles do not all have the same magnitude.

questions.correct_answer: BIBO stable because every pole has negative real part, even though one pole is repeated.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Factor the denominator to get poles at $s=-1$ (repeated), $s=-0.2$, and $s=-3$. Every pole has a negative real part, so the all-poles test says the causal LTI system is BIBO stable.

prompt_blocks.text: Determine BIBO stability of $H(s)=\frac{4}{(s+2)(s-1)(s+5)}$ for a causal LTI system.

choice_blocks.text: Unstable because one pole is in the right half-plane.
BIBO stable because the two left-half-plane poles outweigh the one right-half-plane pole.
BIBO stable because the pole at $s=1$ is only one pole.
Unstable only if more than one pole is in the right half-plane.
BIBO stable because the numerator is constant, so the zeros do not matter.

questions.correct_answer: Unstable because one pole is in the right half-plane.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The denominator gives poles at $s=-2$, $s=1$, and $s=-5$. The pole at $s=1$ has positive real part, so the all-poles test fails and the causal LTI system is not BIBO stable.

entries.lesson_core_move: Identify right-half-plane poles by using their positive real parts to infer growing exponential modes and BIBO instability in causal LTI systems.

sections.section_title: Identifying a Positive Real Pole

prompt_blocks.text: Classify $H(s)=\frac{5}{s-3}$ as stable or unstable in a causal LTI setting.

choice_blocks.text: Stable, because the numerator $5$ is positive.
Unstable, because the pole is at $s=3$ and $\Re\{s\}=3>0$.
Stable, because the pole at $s=3$ is on the imaginary axis.
Stable, because a single pole always gives a decaying mode.
Unstable only if the numerator were negative.

questions.correct_answer: Unstable, because the pole is at $s=3$ and $\Re\{s\}=3>0$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Set the denominator equal to zero: $s-3=0$, so the pole is $s=3$.
Since $\Re\{s\}=3>0$, the pole is in the right-half-plane. A causal LTI system with a right-half-plane pole is BIBO unstable.

prompt_blocks.text: Classify $H(s)=\frac{2}{s+6}$ as stable or unstable in a causal LTI setting.

choice_blocks.text: Unstable, because the pole is at $s=6$ and has positive real part.
Unstable, because the numerator $2$ is positive.
Stable, because the pole is at $s=-6$ and $\Re\{s\}=-6<0$.
Unstable, because any real pole causes a growing exponential.
Stable only because there is no imaginary part in the pole.

questions.correct_answer: Stable, because the pole is at $s=-6$ and $\Re\{s\}=-6<0$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Set the denominator equal to zero: $s+6=0$, so the pole is $s=-6$.
Since $\Re\{s\}=-6<0$, the pole is in the left-half-plane. This first-order causal LTI system has no right-half-plane pole, so it is BIBO stable.

sections.section_title: Classifying a Transfer Function with One Right-Half-Plane Pole

prompt_blocks.text: Classify the stability of $H(s)=\frac{2}{(s-2)(s+1)}$ for a causal LTI system.

choice_blocks.text: Stable, because the numerator is positive.
Stable, because one pole is in the left half-plane.
Unstable, because the pole at $s=2$ is in the right half-plane.
Stable, because the pole magnitudes $2$ and $1$ are finite.
Unstable only if the two poles are complex conjugates.

questions.correct_answer: Unstable, because the pole at $s=2$ is in the right half-plane.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The denominator is zero when $s=2$ or $s=-1$. Since $\Re\{2\}=2>0$, the transfer function has one right-half-plane pole.
For a causal LTI system, one right-half-plane pole is enough to make the system BIBO unstable.

prompt_blocks.text: Classify the stability of $G(s)=\frac{4}{(s-3)(s+5)}$ for a causal LTI system.

choice_blocks.text: Stable, because $s=-5$ is in the left half-plane.
Unstable, because the pole at $s=3$ is in the right half-plane.
Stable, because the numerator constant $4$ does not contain $s$.
Stable, because the larger pole magnitude is associated with $s=-5$.
Unstable only if both poles are in the right half-plane.

questions.correct_answer: Unstable, because the pole at $s=3$ is in the right half-plane.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The poles are found from $(s-3)(s+5)=0$, so $s=3$ and $s=-5$.
Because $\Re\{3\}=3>0$, one pole lies in the right half-plane. Therefore the causal LTI system is BIBO unstable.

sections.section_title: Detecting Right-Half-Plane Poles Among Multiple Poles

prompt_blocks.text: Classify $H(s)=\frac{7(s+1)}{(s+1)(s-1)(s+4)}$ for BIBO stability as a causal LTI system.

choice_blocks.text: Unstable, because $s=1$ is a right-half-plane pole.
Stable, because two denominator factors give left-half-plane pole locations.
Stable, because the zero at $s=-1$ is in the left half-plane.
Unstable, because $s=-4$ has the largest pole-location magnitude.
Stable, because the repeated factor $(s+1)$ in the numerator and denominator decides the classification.

questions.correct_answer: Unstable, because $s=1$ is a right-half-plane pole.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Scan the denominator factors and check the real-part signs. The factor $(s-1)$ gives $s=1$, so $\Re\{1\}=1>0$.
One right-half-plane pole is enough to make a causal LTI system BIBO unstable; the left-half-plane locations do not override it.

prompt_blocks.text: Classify $G(s)=\frac{5(s-2)}{(s+2)(s+6)(s+8)}$ for BIBO stability as a causal LTI system.

choice_blocks.text: Unstable, because the zero at $s=2$ is in the right half-plane.
Stable, because the poles are $s=-2$, $s=-6$, and $s=-8$.
Unstable, because the denominator has three factors.
Unstable, because $s=-8$ has the largest pole-location magnitude.
Stable only because the numerator coefficient $5$ is positive.

questions.correct_answer: Stable, because the poles are $s=-2$, $s=-6$, and $s=-8$, so no pole is in the right half-plane.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Set the denominator factors to zero: the poles are $s=-2$, $s=-6$, and $s=-8$.
Each pole has a negative real part, while the right-half-plane zero at $s=2$ is not a pole. With no right-half-plane poles, this causal LTI system is BIBO stable.

sections.section_title: Recognizing Right-Half-Plane Complex Poles

prompt_blocks.text: For a causal LTI system, classify $H(s)=\frac{8}{(s-(1+j))(s-(1-j))}$ and identify the sign driver.

choice_blocks.text: Unstable; the poles at $1+j$ and $1-j$ have positive real part $+1$.
Stable; complex-conjugate poles are stable whenever the poles are not real.
Stable; the imaginary parts $+1$ and $-1$ only mean oscillation.
Marginally stable; oscillatory factors imply no growth or decay.
Stable; instability would require repeated right-half-plane factors.

questions.correct_answer: Unstable because both poles have real part $+1>0$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Set each denominator factor to zero to find the poles.
Both poles have positive real part, $\Re\{1+j\}=\Re\{1-j\}=1$. For a causal LTI system, any pole with positive real part produces a growing mode, so the system is BIBO unstable.

prompt_blocks.text: For the causal LTI transfer function $H(s)=\frac{5}{(s-(3+2j))(s-(3-2j))}$, which statement is correct?

choice_blocks.text: Stable; the pair is complex, so it represents bounded oscillation.
Unstable; both poles have real part $3>0$, so the modes grow while oscillating.
Stable; the negative imaginary pole cancels the positive imaginary pole.
Stable; a second-order denominator has even degree.
Marginally stable; only the imaginary parts $+2$ and $-2$ determine stability.

questions.correct_answer: Unstable because the complex-conjugate poles are $3\pm 2j$, and their real part is $3>0$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The denominator factors identify the poles directly.

Their real parts are positive: $\Re\{3+2j\}=\Re\{3-2j\}=3$. The imaginary parts set the oscillation frequency, but the positive real part sets growing amplitude, so the causal LTI system is BIBO unstable.

entries.lesson_core_move: Classify imaginary-axis poles by recognizing their nondecaying response modes and marking causal LTI systems with such poles as not BIBO stable.

sections.section_title: Recognizing Poles with Zero Real Part

prompt_blocks.text: Classify the causal LTI transfer function with poles at $-1$, $-3$, $2j$, and $-2j$.

choice_blocks.text: The poles $2j$ and $-2j$ are imaginary-axis poles, so the system is not BIBO stable.
All poles have nonpositive real part, so the system is BIBO stable.
Only $-1$ and $-3$ matter because they are real poles, so the system is BIBO stable.
The poles $-1$ and $-3$ are imaginary-axis poles because their imaginary parts are zero.
The system is BIBO stable because none of the poles have positive real part.

questions.correct_answer: The correct classification is that $2j$ and $-2j$ have zero real part, so they are imaginary-axis poles and the causal LTI system is not BIBO stable.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Check real parts directly: $\Re\{-1\}=-1$, $\Re\{-3\}=-3$, $\Re\{2j\}=0$, and $\Re\{-2j\}=0$.
The poles with $\Re\{p\}=0$ are $p=\pm 2j$. Imaginary-axis poles produce nondecaying modes, so this causal LTI system is not BIBO stable.

prompt_blocks.text: Classify the causal LTI transfer function with poles at $-4$, $-6$, $j$, and $-j$.

choice_blocks.text: The poles $j$ and $-j$ are imaginary-axis poles, so the system is not BIBO stable.
The system is BIBO stable because $-4$ and $-6$ are in the left half-plane.
The poles $j$ and $-j$ are stable because their magnitudes are both $1$.
The poles $-4$ and $-6$ are the imaginary-axis poles because their imaginary parts are zero.
The system is BIBO stable because every pole satisfies $\Re\{p\}\le 0$.

questions.correct_answer: The correct classification is that $j$ and $-j$ have zero real part, so they are imaginary-axis poles and the causal LTI system is not BIBO stable.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Compute the real parts: $\Re\{-4\}=-4$, $\Re\{-6\}=-6$, $\Re\{j\}=0$, and $\Re\{-j\}=0$.
Because $j$ and $-j$ satisfy $\Re\{p\}=0$, they lie on the imaginary axis. A causal LTI system with any imaginary-axis pole is not BIBO stable in this lesson chain.

sections.section_title: Classifying a Pole at the Origin

prompt_blocks.text: Classify $H(s)=\dfrac{1}{s(s+2)(s+5)}$ for BIBO stability.

choice_blocks.text: Not BIBO stable, because $s=0$ is an imaginary-axis pole.
BIBO stable, because no pole has positive real part.
BIBO stable, because the numerator is constant.
BIBO stable, because the two LHP poles dominate the pole at the origin.
BIBO stable, because the denominator has three first-order factors.

questions.correct_answer: Not BIBO stable, because $s=0$ is an imaginary-axis pole.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The denominator gives poles $0$, $-2$, and $-5$. Since $\Re\{0\}=0$, the pole at the origin is on the imaginary axis. A causal LTI system with any imaginary-axis pole is not BIBO stable.

prompt_blocks.text: A causal LTI transfer function has poles at $\{0,-3,-6\}$. Classify its BIBO stability.

choice_blocks.text: BIBO stable, because all nonzero poles are in the LHP.
Not BIBO stable, because $p=0$ has $\Re\{p\}=0$.
BIBO stable, because there are more LHP poles than imaginary-axis poles.
BIBO stable, because a pole at the origin counts as neither stable nor unstable.
BIBO stable, because stability is decided only by the most negative pole.

questions.correct_answer: Not BIBO stable, because $p=0$ has $\Re\{p\}=0$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Check each pole by real part: $\Re\{0\}=0$, $\Re\{-3\}=-3$, and $\Re\{-6\}=-6$. The origin pole is a boundary imaginary-axis pole, so it contributes a nondecaying mode and the causal LTI system is not BIBO stable.

sections.section_title: Classifying Simple Nonzero Imaginary-Axis Poles

prompt_blocks.text: For a causal LTI system, determine whether $H(s)=\dfrac{5}{(s+4)(s-j3)(s+j3)}$ is BIBO stable.

choice_blocks.text: Not BIBO stable; the poles at $p=\pm j3$ have real part $0$ and produce nondecaying oscillatory modes.
BIBO stable; the poles at $p=\pm j3$ are only oscillatory, so they are allowed.
BIBO stable; the nonreal poles form a conjugate pair, so their effects cancel.
Not BIBO stable; the left-half-plane pole at $p=-4$ is the pole that violates stability.
BIBO stable; there are no right-half-plane poles, so the imaginary-axis poles do not matter.

questions.correct_answer: Not BIBO stable, because $p=\pm j3$ are nonzero imaginary-axis poles with $\Re\{p\}=0$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The poles are $p=-4$, $p=j3$, and $p=-j3$. For a causal LTI system, BIBO stability requires all poles to lie strictly in the left half-plane.
The pair $p=\pm j3$ lies on the imaginary axis, so it contributes nondecaying oscillations and the system is not BIBO stable.

prompt_blocks.text: A causal LTI transfer function has poles $\{-5,\,1,\,-j2,\,j2\}$. Which classification is correct?

choice_blocks.text: Not BIBO stable; $p=1$ is in the right half-plane and $p=\pm j2$ are nonzero imaginary-axis poles.
BIBO stable; the two imaginary-axis poles form a conjugate pair and the real poles are finite.
Not BIBO stable only because $p=1$ is in the right half-plane; the poles $p=\pm j2$ would be allowed.
BIBO stable; the imaginary parts have equal magnitude, so the pole set is balanced.
Not BIBO stable because there are four poles; any fourth-order causal system is unstable.

questions.correct_answer: Not BIBO stable: $p=1$ has positive real part, and $p=\pm j2$ are nondecaying imaginary-axis poles.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Classify each pole by real part, because the stability rule depends on whether poles are strictly in the left half-plane.
The pole $p=1$ is in the right half-plane, and the pair $p=\pm j2$ lies on the imaginary axis. Either condition prevents BIBO stability for the causal LTI system.

sections.section_title: Classifying Repeated Imaginary-Axis Poles

prompt_blocks.text: Classify the stability of $H(s)=\dfrac{1}{(s-j1)^2(s+3)}$ for a causal LTI system.

choice_blocks.text: BIBO stable, because the repeated pole is not in the right half-plane.
Not BIBO stable, because the repeated pole at $s=j1$ lies on $\Re\{s\}=0$.
BIBO stable, because the pole at $s=-3$ is in the left half-plane.
BIBO stable only if the repeated pole is counted once.
Not BIBO stable only because repeated poles are always unstable, regardless of location.

questions.correct_answer: Not BIBO stable, because the repeated pole at $s=j1$ lies on $\Re\{s\}=0$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The pole $s=j1$ has real part $0$ and appears with multiplicity $2$. A causal LTI system needs all poles strictly in the left half-plane for BIBO stability, so this system is not BIBO stable.

prompt_blocks.text: Classify the stability of $H(s)=\dfrac{4}{(s+j5)^3(s+2)}$ for a causal LTI system.

choice_blocks.text: Not BIBO stable, because the repeated pole at $s=-j5$ lies on $\Re\{s\}=0$.
BIBO stable, because $s=-j5$ is negative imaginary.
BIBO stable, because the real pole $s=-2$ is in the left half-plane.
BIBO stable, because repeated imaginary-axis poles count as oscillatory but bounded.
Not BIBO stable only if there is also a right-half-plane pole.

questions.correct_answer: Not BIBO stable, because the repeated pole at $s=-j5$ lies on $\Re\{s\}=0$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The repeated pole $s=-j5$ has real part $0$. The additional pole $s=-2$ is stable by itself, but the imaginary-axis pole violates the strict left-half-plane condition, so the causal system is not BIBO stable.

entries.lesson_core_move: Interpret negative real pole locations as decaying exponential response terms and connect their decay rates to stable causal LTI system behavior.

sections.section_title: Finding the Exponential Response from a Negative Real Pole

prompt_blocks.text: Given $H(s)=\frac{4}{s+5}$, what is the matching causal response term?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Match $H(s)$ to $\frac{K}{s+\alpha}$. Here $K=4$ and $\alpha=5$, so the causal response is $K e^{-\alpha t}u(t)=4e^{-5t}u(t)$.

prompt_blocks.text: Given $H(s)=\frac{9}{s+2}$, what is the matching causal response term?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The denominator $s+2$ gives $\alpha=2$ in $\frac{K}{s+\alpha}$, and the numerator gives $K=9$. Therefore the causal decaying exponential term is $9e^{-2t}u(t)$.

sections.section_title: Comparing Decay Rates from Negative Real Pole Locations

prompt_blocks.text: Which pole gives the slowest response decay: $s=-1$, $s=-4$, or $s=-0.5$?

choice_blocks.text: $s=-4$, because the largest magnitude always means the slowest decay.
$s=-0.5$, because $e^{-0.5t}u(t)$ has the smallest positive decay rate.
$s=-1$, because it is between the other two pole locations.
All three poles give the same decay rate because they are all negative.
None of the poles gives decay because negative real poles are unstable.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A pole at $s=-a$ gives a decaying exponential with positive decay rate $a$. The rates are $1$, $4$, and $0.5$, so the smallest rate is $0.5$. Therefore $s=-0.5$ produces the slowest decay.

prompt_blocks.text: For $H_1(s)=3/(s+2)$ and $H_2(s)=3/(s+5)$, which response term decays faster?

choice_blocks.text: $3e^{-2t}u(t)$ decays faster because $s=-2$ is closer to the origin.
$3e^{-5t}u(t)$ decays faster because its decay rate is $5$.
The two terms decay at the same rate because both numerators are $3$.
$3e^{2t}u(t)$ decays faster because the pole sign changes in time.
Neither term is stable because negative real poles create growing exponentials.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: $H_1(s)=3/(s+2)$ corresponds to $3e^{-2t}u(t)$, and $H_2(s)=3/(s+5)$ corresponds to $3e^{-5t}u(t)$. Since $5>2$, the term with rate $5$ decays faster.

sections.section_title: Interpreting Multiple Negative Real Poles as Decaying Terms

prompt_blocks.text: For a causal LTI system with $H(s)=\frac{4}{s+2}+\frac{1}{s+6}$, which response correctly keeps the two negative real poles as separate decaying terms?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Apply the causal single-pole map $\frac{K}{s+\alpha}\mapsto Ke^{-\alpha t}u(t)$ to each summand separately. The poles at $-2$ and $-6$ give decay rates $2$ and $6$, so the response is the sum $4e^{-2t}u(t)+e^{-6t}u(t)$.

prompt_blocks.text: Given $H(s)=\frac{5}{s+3}+\frac{2}{s+8}$ for a causal response, which option gives the correct time-domain terms and decay rates?

choice_blocks.text: $h(t)=5e^{-3t}u(t)+2e^{-8t}u(t)$, with decay rates $3$ and $8$.
$h(t)=7e^{-11t}u(t)$, with decay rate $11$.
$h(t)=5e^{3t}u(t)+2e^{8t}u(t)$, with growth rates $3$ and $8$.
$h(t)=5e^{-8t}u(t)+2e^{-3t}u(t)$, with decay rates $8$ and $3$.
$h(t)=3e^{-5t}u(t)+8e^{-2t}u(t)$, with decay rates $5$ and $2$.

questions.correct_answer: $h(t)=5e^{-3t}u(t)+2e^{-8t}u(t)$, with decay rates $3$ and $8$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Each term maps independently: $\frac{5}{s+3}$ becomes $5e^{-3t}u(t)$, and $\frac{2}{s+8}$ becomes $2e^{-8t}u(t)$. The decay rate comes from the positive number added to $s$ in each denominator, so the rates are $3$ and $8$.

sections.section_title: Connecting Decaying Exponential Responses to BIBO Stability

prompt_blocks.text: For $H(s)=\frac{5}{s+2}-\frac{1}{s+6}$, classify the causal system as BIBO stable or unstable.

choice_blocks.text: BIBO stable, because both poles are negative real and both exponential terms decay.
BIBO unstable, because the coefficient on $\frac{1}{s+6}$ is negative.
BIBO unstable, because the two decay rates are different.
BIBO stable only if the two terms cancel exactly.
BIBO unstable, because rational transfer functions with two separate terms require repeated poles to be stable.

questions.correct_answer: BIBO stable, because the poles are $s=-2$ and $s=-6$, so the causal impulse response is a finite sum of decaying exponentials.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The poles are $s=-2$ and $s=-6$, both in the left half-plane. The negative coefficient changes the sign of one response term, but it does not change the fact that both terms decay for $t\ge 0$.

prompt_blocks.text: For $H(s)=\frac{3}{s+4}+\frac{2}{s-1}$, classify the causal system as BIBO stable or unstable.

choice_blocks.text: BIBO unstable, because the pole at $s=1$ gives a growing exponential term.
BIBO stable, because the pole at $s=-4$ gives a decaying exponential term.
BIBO stable, because both coefficients $3$ and $2$ are positive.
BIBO unstable, because the denominator factors are not repeated.
BIBO stable, because a finite sum of two rational terms is always bounded.

questions.correct_answer: BIBO unstable, because $s=1$ is a right-half-plane pole and produces the growing term $2e^{t}u(t)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The pole at $s=-4$ gives a decaying mode, but the pole at $s=1$ gives $e^{t}u(t)$, which grows instead of decaying. One growing mode is enough to make the causal system BIBO unstable.

entries.lesson_core_move: Identify positive real pole contributions as growing exponential response terms and use their unbounded time-domain growth to classify a causal LTI system as BIBO unstable.

sections.section_title: Identifying Positive Real Pole Contributions

prompt_blocks.text: For the transfer function below, which pole creates a growing exponential contribution in the causal impulse response?

choice_blocks.text: $s=3$, so a term proportional to $e^{3t}u(t)$ is growing.
$s=-2$, so a term proportional to $e^{-2t}u(t)$ is growing.
$s=-5$, so a term proportional to $e^{-5t}u(t)$ is growing.
There is no growing contribution because the denominator is already factored.
All three poles create growing contributions.

questions.correct_answer: $s=3$, which gives a growing candidate proportional to $e^{3t}u(t)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Solve each denominator factor for its pole: $(s-3)=0$ gives $s=3$, $(s+2)=0$ gives $s=-2$, and $(s+5)=0$ gives $s=-5$.
Only the positive real pole $s=3$ has a positive exponent in the causal response, so it is the growing contribution candidate.

prompt_blocks.text: For the transfer function below, identify the pole that produces the growing exponential contribution.

choice_blocks.text: $s=2$, giving a growing candidate proportional to $e^{2t}u(t)$.
$s=-1$, because the repeated pole creates the growing contribution.
$s=-4$, because it has the largest magnitude.
$s=-1$ and $s=-4$, because both come from factors with plus signs.
There is no growing contribution because the numerator is negative.

questions.correct_answer: $s=2$, which gives a growing candidate proportional to $e^{2t}u(t)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The denominator factors give poles at $s=-1$ with repetition, $s=2$, and $s=-4$.
The repeated pole at $s=-1$ is still negative, and $s=-4$ is also negative. The only positive real pole is $s=2$, so it is the growing contribution candidate.

sections.section_title: Converting a Positive Real Pole to a Growing Exponential Response

prompt_blocks.text: For the causal transfer block $H(s)=\frac{4}{s-2}$, which time-domain term is the growing exponential response?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Match $H(s)$ to $\frac{A}{s-a}$. Here $A=4$ and $a=2$, so the causal inverse-Laplace term is $Ae^{at}u(t)=4e^{2t}u(t)$.
Because $2>0$, this exponential grows without bound as $t\to\infty$.

prompt_blocks.text: For a causal system with $H(s)=\frac{3}{s-4}+\frac{7}{s+1}$, which term is the unstable growing contribution in $h(t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The positive real pole is $s=4$, and its residue is $3$. The term $\frac{3}{s-4}$ therefore converts to $3e^{4t}u(t)$ for a causal system.
The term from $s=-1$ is $7e^{-t}u(t)$, which decays, so it is not the unstable growing contribution.

sections.section_title: Classifying Instability from an Unbounded Exponential Term

prompt_blocks.text: Determine the BIBO stability classification for $h(t)=4e^{t}u(t)-3e^{-2t}u(t)+u(t)$, and identify the term that determines the classification.

choice_blocks.text: BIBO unstable; the unstable contribution is $4e^{t}u(t)$.
BIBO stable; the decaying term $-3e^{-2t}u(t)$ dominates for large $t$.
BIBO stable; all coefficients are finite constants.
BIBO unstable; the unstable contribution is $u(t)$.
BIBO stable; a system is stable as long as at least one term decays.

questions.correct_answer: BIBO unstable; the unstable contribution is $4e^{t}u(t)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The term $4e^{t}u(t)$ has a positive exponent, so it grows without bound as $t$ increases. One unbounded causal exponential term is enough to make the impulse response fail the BIBO stability test, regardless of the decaying or bounded companion terms.

prompt_blocks.text: Determine the BIBO stability classification for $h(t)=-6e^{3t}u(t)+2e^{-t}u(t)-7e^{-4t}u(t)$, and identify the term that determines the classification.

choice_blocks.text: BIBO stable; the two decaying terms outweigh the growing term.
BIBO unstable; the unstable contribution is $-6e^{3t}u(t)$.
BIBO stable; the negative coefficient on $-6e^{3t}u(t)$ prevents unbounded growth.
BIBO unstable; the unstable contribution is $2e^{-t}u(t)$.
BIBO stable; only a positive coefficient can make an exponential term unstable.

questions.correct_answer: BIBO unstable; the unstable contribution is $-6e^{3t}u(t)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The exponent in $e^{3t}$ is positive, so the magnitude of $-6e^{3t}u(t)$ grows without bound for large positive $t$. The sign of the coefficient does not make the term bounded, and one growing causal exponential term makes the system BIBO unstable.

sections.section_title: Classifying Mixed Pole Sets with One Growing Exponential Contribution

prompt_blocks.text: For the causal LTI system with $H(s)=\frac{4(s+2)}{(s-4)(s+3)(s^2+6s+13)}$, which classification and unstable contribution are correct?

choice_blocks.text: The system is **BIBO unstable** because the pole at $s=4$ contributes a growing term of the form $A e^{4t}u(t)$.
The system is BIBO stable because the poles from $s^2+6s+13$ have negative real part.
The system is BIBO unstable because the complex poles contribute $A e^{3t}\cos(2t)u(t)$.
The system is BIBO stable because the numerator factor $s+2$ removes the growing pole.
The system is BIBO unstable because the pole at $s=-3$ contributes $A e^{-3t}u(t)$.

questions.correct_answer: The system is **BIBO unstable** because the positive-real pole $s=4$ contributes $A e^{4t}u(t)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The denominator gives poles $s=4$, $s=-3$, and $s=-3\pm j2$. Only $s=4$ has positive real part, so the causal response contains a growing term $A e^{4t}u(t)$. One growing term is enough to make the system BIBO unstable.

prompt_blocks.text: For the causal LTI system with $H(s)=\frac{7(s+1)}{(s+2)(s-5)(s^2+8s+20)}$, which option correctly identifies the stability result and decisive time-domain term?

choice_blocks.text: The system is BIBO stable because the quadratic poles are $s=-4\pm j2$.
The system is **BIBO unstable** because the pole at $s=5$ contributes a growing term of the form $A e^{5t}u(t)$.
The system is BIBO unstable because the pole at $s=-2$ contributes $A e^{2t}u(t)$.
The system is BIBO stable because the average of the real parts $5$, $-2$, and $-4$ is negative.
The system is BIBO unstable because the quadratic contributes $A e^{4t}\cos(2t)u(t)$.

questions.correct_answer: The system is **BIBO unstable** because the pole $s=5$ contributes $A e^{5t}u(t)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The poles are $s=-2$, $s=5$, and $s=-4\pm j2$. The stable terms do not cancel the effect of $s=5$: a causal pole with positive real part produces a growing exponential contribution $A e^{5t}u(t)$, so the system is BIBO unstable.

entries.lesson_core_move: Convert left-half-plane complex-conjugate pole locations into exponentially decaying sinusoidal response terms and their BIBO-stable causal LTI interpretation.

sections.section_title: Identifying Decaying Oscillations from Left-Half-Plane Pole Pairs

prompt_blocks.text: Given pole pairs $s=-1\pm j2$, $s=2\pm j1$, and $s=-3\pm j4$, which classification is correct?

choice_blocks.text: $s=-1\pm j2$ and $s=-3\pm j4$ are decaying oscillatory; $s=2\pm j1$ is unstable oscillatory.
All three pairs are decaying oscillatory because all three have nonzero imaginary parts.
Only $s=-1\pm j2$ is decaying oscillatory; $s=2\pm j1$ and $s=-3\pm j4$ are unstable oscillatory.
$s=2\pm j1$ is decaying oscillatory; $s=-1\pm j2$ and $s=-3\pm j4$ are unstable oscillatory.
$s=-1\pm j2$ is sustained oscillatory, $s=2\pm j1$ is decaying oscillatory, and $s=-3\pm j4$ is non-oscillatory.

questions.correct_answer: $s=-1\pm j2$ and $s=-3\pm j4$ are decaying oscillatory; $s=2\pm j1$ is unstable oscillatory.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A decaying oscillatory pair must be complex, conjugate, and have negative real part. The pairs with real parts $-1$ and $-3$ satisfy this, while the pair with real part $2$ grows for a causal LTI response.

answer_explanation_blocks.latex: s=-1\pm j2 \Rightarrow \sigma=-1<0,\quad s=2\pm j1 \Rightarrow \sigma=2>0,\quad s=-3\pm j4 \Rightarrow \sigma=-3<0

prompt_blocks.text: For the pole cases $s=-4\pm j5$, $s=-2$, $s=\pm j6$, and $s=1\pm j3$, which statement correctly identifies the decaying oscillatory contributors?

choice_blocks.text: Only $s=-4\pm j5$ is decaying oscillatory; $s=-2$ is non-oscillatory, $s=\pm j6$ is sustained oscillatory, and $s=1\pm j3$ is unstable oscillatory.
$s=-4\pm j5$ and $s=\pm j6$ are both decaying oscillatory because both are complex conjugate pairs.
$s=-2$ is the only decaying oscillatory contributor because it has a negative real part.
$s=1\pm j3$ is decaying oscillatory because its imaginary part is nonzero.
None of the cases are decaying oscillatory because a decaying oscillation cannot come from complex poles.

questions.correct_answer: Only $s=-4\pm j5$ is decaying oscillatory.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The pair $s=-4\pm j5$ is complex, conjugate, and has negative real part, so it gives a decaying oscillation. The pole $s=-2$ decays without oscillating, $s=\pm j6$ oscillates without decay, and $s=1\pm j3$ grows because its real part is positive.

sections.section_title: Reading Decay Rate and Oscillation Frequency from Complex Poles

prompt_blocks.text: For poles $s=-4\pm j5$, which pair gives the decay constant and angular oscillation frequency?

choice_blocks.text: Decay constant $4$, angular frequency $5$
Decay constant $5$, angular frequency $4$
Decay constant $-4$, angular frequency $5$
Decay constant $5$, angular frequency $-4$
Two real decay constants $4$ and $5$, with no oscillation frequency

questions.correct_answer: Decay constant $4$ and angular frequency $5$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Match $s=-4\pm j5$ to $s=\sigma\pm j\omega$. The real part is $\sigma=-4$, so the exponential envelope is $e^{-4t}$ and the decay constant is $4$. The imaginary coefficient is $\omega=5$, so the angular frequency is $5$.

prompt_blocks.text: A causal LTI response has a complex-conjugate pole pair $s=-7\pm j3$. Which time-domain prototype uses the correct decay rate and oscillation frequency?

choice_blocks.text: $e^{-7t}\left(A\cos(3t)+B\sin(3t)\right)u(t)$
$e^{-3t}\left(A\cos(7t)+B\sin(7t)\right)u(t)$
$e^{7t}\left(A\cos(3t)+B\sin(3t)\right)u(t)$
$e^{-7t}\left(A\cos(7t)+B\sin(7t)\right)u(t)$

questions.correct_answer: $e^{-7t}\left(A\cos(3t)+B\sin(3t)\right)u(t)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The pair $s=-7\pm j3$ has real part $-7$ and imaginary coefficient $3$. Therefore the decay constant is $7$, giving $e^{-7t}$, and the oscillation frequency is $3$, giving the sinusoidal terms with argument $3t$.

sections.section_title: Writing the Response Term from a Complex-Conjugate Pole Pair

prompt_blocks.text: A transfer factor contributes poles at $s=-3\pm j4$. Choose the corresponding causal decaying oscillatory response term.

choice_blocks.text: $h_c(t)=e^{-3t}\left(A\cos(4t)+B\sin(4t)\right)u(t)$
$h_c(t)=e^{3t}\left(A\cos(4t)+B\sin(4t)\right)u(t)$
$h_c(t)=A\cos(4t)+B\sin(4t)$
$h_c(t)=e^{-3t}\left(A\cos(4t)+B\sin(4t)\right)$
$h_c(t)=e^{-4t}\left(A\cos(3t)+B\sin(3t)\right)u(t)$

questions.correct_answer: $h_c(t)=e^{-3t}\left(A\cos(4t)+B\sin(4t)\right)u(t)$

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The pole pair $s=-3\pm j4$ gives $\alpha=3$ and $\omega=4$, so the causal real response mode is $e^{-3t}\left(A\cos(4t)+B\sin(4t)\right)u(t)$.

prompt_blocks.text: A denominator factor is $(s+6)^2+9$. Choose the corresponding causal decaying oscillatory response term.

choice_blocks.text: $h_c(t)=e^{6t}\left(A\cos(3t)+B\sin(3t)\right)u(t)$
$h_c(t)=e^{-6t}\left(A\cos(3t)+B\sin(3t)\right)u(t)$
$h_c(t)=A\cos(3t)+B\sin(3t)$
$h_c(t)=e^{-6t}\left(A\cos(3t)+B\sin(3t)\right)$
$h_c(t)=e^{-3t}\left(A\cos(6t)+B\sin(6t)\right)u(t)$

questions.correct_answer: $h_c(t)=e^{-6t}\left(A\cos(3t)+B\sin(3t)\right)u(t)$

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Match $(s+6)^2+9$ to $(s+\alpha)^2+\omega^2$. This gives $\alpha=6$ and $\omega=3$, so the causal mode is $e^{-6t}\left(A\cos(3t)+B\sin(3t)\right)u(t)$.

sections.section_title: Interpreting BIBO Stability from Decaying Oscillatory Modes

prompt_blocks.text: A causal LTI system has impulse-response modes $e^{-3t}(2\cos 5t)u(t)$, $e^{-t}(4\sin 2t)u(t)$, and $e^{0.5t}(\cos t)u(t)$. What is the correct BIBO stability conclusion?

choice_blocks.text: BIBO stable, because two of the three modes have decaying exponential envelopes.
BIBO stable, because the oscillatory factors $\cos(5t)$, $\sin(2t)$, and $\cos(t)$ are bounded.
Unstable, because the mode with envelope $e^{0.5t}$ has a positive real exponent.
Marginally stable, because oscillation prevents the response from settling to a constant.
Non-causal, because the pole locations are not written explicitly as a denominator.

questions.correct_answer: Unstable, because the mode with envelope $e^{0.5t}$ has a positive real exponent.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: For a causal LTI system, BIBO stability requires every mode envelope to decay as $t \to +\infty$. The real exponents here are $-3$, $-1$, and $+0.5$, so the positive exponent produces a growing oscillatory mode.

prompt_blocks.text: A causal LTI system has modes $e^{-2t}(3\cos 4t)u(t)$, $e^{-0.75t}(\sin 6t)u(t)$, and $e^{-5t}(2\cos t)u(t)$. What is the correct BIBO stability conclusion?

choice_blocks.text: BIBO stable, because all three exponential envelopes decay.
Unstable, because any oscillatory mode makes the output unbounded.
Unstable, because the mode with $\sin(6t)$ has the largest oscillation frequency.
Marginally stable, because the system contains sinusoidal factors.
Non-causal, because the response terms do not include an explicit transfer-function denominator.

questions.correct_answer: BIBO stable, because all three exponential envelopes decay.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The real exponents are $-2$, $-0.75$, and $-5$. Since each real part is negative, every oscillatory mode is exponentially decaying, so the causal LTI system is BIBO stable.
